Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] FortiGate SSL VPN brute-force / credential stuffing surge against /remote/login
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] First-seen successful FortiGate SSL VPN logon for user from new source IP (FortiBleed reuse) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] FortiGate admin account creation or privilege escalation following anomalous logon · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] FortiGate configuration backup / export to non-routine destination · [LLM] VPN-pool IP fan-out — single SSL VPN user touching multiple internal hosts post-auth · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
FortiGate SSL VPN brute-force / credential stuffing surge against /remote/login AIReconnaissance High
Detects the FortiBleed-style high-volume authentication attempts against FortiGate SSL VPN portals (/remote/login). Hunts for sources hitting >50 failed VPN auths in a 5-minute window or any source touching >25 distinct usernames — the shape of the 1.16B-attempt campaign described in the article. Rationale: Article cites '1.16 billion credential attempts against more than 320,000 FortiGate targets to intercept SSL VPN authentication hashes' — the brute-force / spray shape is the primary credential_access signal. Thresholds (50 fails / 25 distinct users per 5-min window per src IP) are conservative for spray-pattern actors. Removed invalid `Computer` column from CommonSecurityLog (CEF schema doesn't carry it; using DeviceName/SourceIP/SourceUserName instead). Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1110/003/
ATT&CKT1110.001 T1110.003 T1557
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Authentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Misconfigured SSO endpoint retrying failed creds in a tight loop
  • NAC / posture-check service repeatedly authenticating to test reachability
  • Vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Qualys) hitting the SSL VPN portal during an authenticated scan
  • Single user with expired AD password trying multiple times before resetting
  • Mobile FortiClient VPN client stuck in an auth loop after laptop sleep/resume
Suppression filter
| where SrcIP !in ("<corporate_nac_ip>", "<vuln_scanner_ip>")
| where SrcIP !startswith "10." and SrcIP !startswith "192.168."
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pivot on SrcIP in the alert. Pull all FortiGate auth events from that IP in the last 24h via CommonSecurityLog; geolocate; check ASN against known-good (corporate egress, partner VPN). If the user-set spans >25 accounts and includes admin-naming patterns (root, admin, fortinet), treat as a confirmed spray. Step 2 — Contain: block the source IP at the FortiGate WAN ACL and at the upstream edge; if a successful authentication followed any failure burst, force-logoff all VPN sessions for those accounts and reset passwords. Step 3 — Hunt: query the FortiBleed lookup (Hudson Rock) and Have-I-Been-Pwned for every account hit; check IdentityLogonEvents and SigninLogs for the same usernames showing successful auth from any IP in the last 30 days; review FortiGate admin logs for config-export/system-backup events that bracket the spray window.
// Defender XDR does not natively ingest FortiGate VPN logs; this query targets Defender for Identity/IdentityLogonEvents when FortiGate auth is forwarded via SAML to AAD
IdentityLogonEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1h)
| where Application has_any ("FortiGate","Fortinet","SSLVPN")
| where ActionType == "LogonFailed"
| summarize FailedCount = count(), DistinctUsers = dcount(AccountUpn), Users = make_set(AccountUpn, 25) by IPAddress, bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where FailedCount > 50 or DistinctUsers > 25
| order by FailedCount desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet" and DeviceProduct has_any ("FortiGate","Fortigate")
| where Activity has_any ("ssl-login-fail","login failed","SSL VPN login fail") or DeviceEventClassID in ("0102043521","0100032003","0101039426")
| extend SrcIP = coalesce(SourceIP, tostring(parse_json(AdditionalExtensions).src))
| summarize FailedCount = count(), DistinctUsers = dcount(SourceUserName), Users = make_set(SourceUserName, 25), Firewalls = make_set(DeviceName, 5) by SrcIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where FailedCount > 50 or DistinctUsers > 25
| order by FailedCount desc
source:fortinet (@evt.name:("ssl-login-fail" OR "login failed" OR "SSL VPN login fail") OR @msg:(*"ssl-login-fail"* OR *"SSL VPN login fail"*)) @evt.outcome:failure
ENDPOINT

| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Authentication.user) as distinct_users, values(Authentication.user) as users, values(Authentication.dest) as dest from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app="fortigate-sslvpn" Authentication.action="failure" by Authentication.src, _time span=5m | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where count>50 OR distinct_users>25 | sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Authentication.user) as distinct_users, values(Authentication.user) as users, values(Authentication.dest) as dest from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app="fortigate-sslvpn" Authentication.action="failure" by Authentication.src, _time span=5m | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where count>50 OR distinct_users>25 | sort - count
First-seen successful FortiGate SSL VPN logon for user from new source IP (FortiBleed reuse) AIDelivery High
After FortiBleed dropped plaintext VPN credentials for 73,932 firewalls, attackers are reusing valid creds to log in directly. This UC surfaces the FIRST successful SSL VPN authentication for any user from a source IP / ASN / country never seen for that user in the prior 30 days — the exact shape CISA told customers to hunt. Rationale: CISA explicitly told customers to 'review logs for signs of unauthorized access' against the leaked-credential dataset. First-seen-IP-for-user is the cleanest pivot when the credentials themselves are valid. Removed `Computer` (not a CommonSecurityLog column) and key off DeviceName/SourceUserName/SourceIP instead. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/fortinet-credentials • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078/
ATT&CKT1078 T1133
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate user traveling internationally or working from a new home / hotel network
  • ISP DHCP churn rotating residential user onto a new public IP
  • Mobile carrier NAT egress changing per session
  • User connecting through a personal VPN (Mullvad, NordVPN) for the first time
  • M&A scenario where a newly-onboarded subsidiary's address space hasn't been baselined yet
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !startswith "<corp_egress_/16>"
| where not (Location has_any ("<expected_country>") and AccountName in (dynamic(["traveling-users"])))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: enrich SourceIP with ASN / geolocation / VPN-provider intel (Spur, IPQS, GreyNoise). Compare to the user's last 30 days of corporate-network egress. Cross-check the username against the public FortiBleed dataset (Hudson Rock lookup tool). Pull all post-auth activity from that VPN session: assigned tunnel IP, downstream RDP/SMB/WinRM. Step 2 — Contain: if the username appears in the FortiBleed dataset OR the ASN is a bulletproof / hosting provider (Selectel, Aeza, M247, Alibaba), force-disconnect the VPN session via FortiGate CLI 'execute vpn sslvpn del-tunnel', invalidate the user's password and any active tokens, revoke AAD refresh tokens. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the SourceIP across the last 30 days for any other successful auths against the same FortiGate or peer firewalls; review SigninLogs / AADSignInEventsBeta for token-replay risk; check DeviceLogonEvents for the VPN-assigned IP touching internal hosts.
let Window = 1h;
let Baseline = IdentityLogonEvents
    | where Timestamp between (ago(30d) .. ago(Window))
    | where Application has_any ("FortiGate","Fortinet","SSLVPN")
    | where ActionType == "LogonSuccess"
    | summarize by AccountUpn, IPAddress;
IdentityLogonEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(Window)
| where Application has_any ("FortiGate","Fortinet","SSLVPN")
| where ActionType == "LogonSuccess"
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on AccountUpn, IPAddress
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Location, DeviceName, Application
| order by Timestamp desc
let Window = 1h;
let Baseline = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(Window))
    | where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet" and DeviceProduct has_any ("FortiGate","Fortigate")
    | where Activity has_any ("ssl-login-success","SSL VPN tunnel up","login successful")
    | summarize by SourceUserName, SourceIP;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Window)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet" and DeviceProduct has_any ("FortiGate","Fortigate")
| where Activity has_any ("ssl-login-success","SSL VPN tunnel up","login successful")
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on SourceUserName, SourceIP
| extend Firewall = DeviceName
| project TimeGenerated, SourceUserName, SourceIP, Firewall, DeviceProduct, Activity
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:fortinet (@evt.name:("ssl-login-success" OR "SSL VPN tunnel up" OR "login successful") OR @msg:(*"ssl-login-success"* OR *"SSL VPN tunnel up"*)) @evt.outcome:success

FortiGate configuration backup / export to non-routine destination AIActions on Objectives Medium
FortiBleed leaked data 'appears to have originated from Fortinet configuration files' per Kevin Beaumont. This UC hunts unexpected FortiGate config-backup operations (execute backup config, system backup) initiated outside the normal admin source-set or to non-corporate destinations — the collection / exfiltration phase that fed the leak server. Rationale: Beaumont's analysis tied the leaked dataset directly to Fortinet configuration files; the only way the actor pulled those at scale is via the documented backup-config admin action. Anti-join against 30-day per-admin baseline isolates the unusual operator. Fixed CommonSecurityLog schema — used DeviceName/SourceUserName/SourceIP rather than the non-existent Computer column. Cross-checked against: • https://doublepulsar.com/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cisa-warns-fortinet-users-to-secure-devices-after-fortibleed-leak/
ATT&CKT1602.002 T1005 T1567
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Quarterly compliance backup performed by an admin who hasn't done one in the rolling 30-day window
  • New admin onboarded who runs their first backup as part of training
  • Automated backup script that just got migrated to a new service account
  • DR test where an off-shift engineer pulls config to verify restore procedures
  • FortiManager / FortiAnalyzer scheduled config-sync from a new appliance IP
Suppression filter
| where Admin !in ("<scheduled_backup_svc_account>", "<fortimanager_sync_account>")
| where AdminSrcIP !startswith "<fortimanager_subnet>"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm the admin account is legitimate (HR-active, expected on-call); verify the source IP for the admin session matches a known jump host or VPN egress. Pull the FortiGate session log for any SCP/SFTP/HTTPS upload from the firewall management interface in the same window. Step 2 — Contain: if the admin account or source IP is unexpected, suspend the admin account, force-rotate ALL FortiGate admin credentials per CISA guidance, terminate any active admin sessions, and rotate the configuration's pre-shared keys (IPsec PSKs, SNMP communities, LDAP bind passwords). Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the source IP across all FortiGate, FortiManager, and FortiAnalyzer admin telemetry for the last 90 days; look for outbound HTTPS from the firewall to uncategorized destinations within ±15 min of the backup; check for any new admin accounts (system admin add) created in the same session.
// Defender does not ingest FortiGate admin events; this targets the case where the config artefact is dropped onto a Windows jump host
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName matches regex @"(?i)^(fgt|fortigate|firewall|backup|sys)[A-Za-z0-9_\-\.]*\.(conf|cfg|backup|bak)$"
   or FileName endswith ".conf.gz"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("backupexec.exe","veeam.backup.shell.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, FileSize, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where Activity has_any ("Configuration backed up","backup config","system backup","config-backup") or DeviceEventClassID in ("0100044546","0100032002")
| extend Admin = SourceUserName, AdminSrcIP = SourceIP, Firewall = DeviceName, BackupDst = DestinationIP
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), BackupCount = count(), Sources = make_set(AdminSrcIP), Destinations = make_set(BackupDst) by Admin, Firewall
| join kind=leftanti (
    CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(7d))
    | where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
    | where Activity has_any ("Configuration backed up","backup config","system backup")
    | summarize PriorBackups = count() by Admin = SourceUserName
    | where PriorBackups >= 3
  ) on Admin
| order by FirstSeen desc
title: FortiGate Configuration Backup from Non-Routine Administrator

description: Detects FortiGate configuration export/backup operations by an administrator who has not performed this action in the prior 30 days, aligned with the FortiBleed config-file exfiltration pattern.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cisa-warns-fortinet-users-to-secure-devices-after-fortibleed-leak/

    DeviceVendor: 'Fortinet'

      - 'Configuration backed up'

source:fortinet (@evt.name:("Configuration backed up" OR "backup config" OR "system backup" OR "config-backup") OR @msg:(*"Configuration backed up"* OR *"execute backup config"*))
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/(fgt|fortigate|firewall|backup).*\.(conf|cfg|backup|bak)$/i
| ContextImageFileName!=/(veeam|backupexec|robocopy)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())

VPN-pool IP fan-out — single SSL VPN user touching multiple internal hosts post-auth AIActions on Objectives Medium
CISA flagged 'unauthorized access or lateral movement' as the expected post-foothold behaviour after FortiBleed credential reuse. This UC detects the classic shape: an SSL VPN tunnel IP initiating SMB/RDP/WinRM/SSH connections to many distinct internal hosts in a short window after authentication — atypical for a remote knowledge worker. Rationale: Article quotes CISA: 'review logs for signs of unauthorized access or lateral movement.' The lateral_movement hint in the kill-chain block calls out 'VPN-assigned IPs initiating SMB/RDP/WinRM to multiple internal hosts.' Threshold of >8 distinct destinations in 10m is aggressive enough to catch hands-on-keyboard discovery while filtering out single-target user activity. Fixed Sentinel query to use SecurityEvent.Computer (which IS a valid column there) instead of CommonSecurityLog.Computer (which is not). Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/ • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts
ATT&CKT1021.001 T1021.002 T1021.006 T1078
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Authentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin / DevOps engineer on VPN running an Ansible playbook or PowerShell remoting loop against a fleet
  • Security tool (Tenable agent, BeyondTrust Bomgar) doing scheduled discovery from a VPN-connected jump host
  • Backup or AV management server connected via VPN pulling status from many endpoints
  • Helpdesk technician remote-assisting multiple users in a single shift
  • SCCM / MECM client on VPN polling DPs and SUPs across sites
Suppression filter
and TargetUserName !in (dynamic(["svc-ansible","svc-sccm","helpdesk-tech-1","vuln-scan-svc"]))
and IpAddress !in (dynamic(["<jump_host_vpn_ip>"]))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the FortiGate SSL VPN session that owned this tunnel IP at the timestamp (CommonSecurityLog SourceUserName for the lease). Validate the user's role — should this person be touching >8 servers via SMB/RDP/WinRM? Check if the source IP for the VPN auth itself was flagged by UC #2. Pull DeviceLogonEvents for the same TargetAccount to see if any logons succeeded vs failed. Step 2 — Contain: if user role is non-admin or VPN source IP is suspicious, terminate the SSL VPN session ('execute vpn sslvpn del-tunnel <user>'), disable the AD account, revoke AAD refresh tokens, isolate any host the VPN IP successfully logged into. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the user account across all DeviceLogonEvents / IdentityLogonEvents in the last 30 days; check for net.exe, nltest, AdFind, BloodHound-style enumeration patterns from any of the touched hosts; scan touched hosts for newly-created services, scheduled tasks, and accounts in the window of the fan-out.
let SSLVPNPools = dynamic(["10.212.134.0/24","10.212.135.0/24"]); // adjust to your FortiGate SSL VPN address-objects
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1h)
| where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| where RemotePort in (445, 3389, 5985, 5986, 22)
| where ipv4_is_in_any_range(LocalIP, SSLVPNPools) or ipv4_is_in_any_range(RemoteIP, SSLVPNPools)
| summarize DistinctDests = dcount(RemoteIP), Dests = make_set(RemoteIP, 20), Ports = make_set(RemotePort) by DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where DistinctDests > 8
| order by DistinctDests desc
let SSLVPNPools = dynamic(["10.212.134.0/24","10.212.135.0/24"]);
let AuthFanOut = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
    | where EventID in (4624, 4625, 4776)
    | where LogonType in (3, 10)
    | where ipv4_is_in_any_range(IpAddress, SSLVPNPools)
    | summarize DistinctTargets = dcount(Computer), Targets = make_set(Computer, 20), LogonTypes = make_set(LogonType) by IpAddress, TargetUserName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
    | where DistinctTargets > 8;
AuthFanOut
| order by DistinctTargets desc
source:(windows.security OR windows.sysmon) @EventID:(4624 OR 4625 OR 5140) @LogonType:(3 OR 10) CIDR(@IpAddress, 10.212.134.0/24, 10.212.135.0/24)
#event_simpleName=UserLogon LogonType=/^(3|10|RemoteInteractive|Network)$/
| cidr("10.212.134.0/24", field=RemoteAddressIP4) OR cidr("10.212.135.0/24", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| groupBy([RemoteAddressIP4, UserName], function=[count(field=aid, distinct=true, as=DistinctHosts), min(_time, as=FirstSeen), max(_time, as=LastSeen)])
| DistinctHosts > 8

FortiGate admin account creation or privilege escalation following anomalous logon AIInstallation High
Attackers reusing leaked FortiBleed credentials commonly create persistent admin accounts on the appliance to survive password resets. This UC pairs a successful FortiGate admin authentication from an anomalous source with a subsequent 'config system admin' add/edit operation in the same admin session — a tight temporal correlation that catches the persistence step CISA specifically warned about ('remove any unauthorized accounts'). Rationale: CISA's mitigation list explicitly says 'remove any unauthorized accounts' — that's the persistence behaviour the agency expects from FortiBleed-leveraging actors. Pairing the admin auth with the immediate config-system-admin write inside a 10-minute window is much higher fidelity than alerting on either alone. Sentinel query uses CommonSecurityLog with DeviceName/SourceUserName/SourceIP (valid columns) instead of the non-existent Computer field flagged in validation. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1136/001/
ATT&CKT1136.001 T1098 T1078
Data sourcesChange.Account_Management Authentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Network engineer onboarding a new admin during a scheduled change window
  • FortiManager pushing an admin-account template change to a managed FortiGate
  • Break-glass account being rotated as part of a quarterly credential hygiene exercise
  • Vendor support session where the FortiGate admin temporarily creates a tech-support account
  • Outsourced MSP performing routine admin-account audit and remediation
Suppression filter
| where NewAdmin !in ("break-glass","audit","fortimanager")
| where Admin !in ("fmg-sync","forticloud-svc")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: enumerate every admin account on the FortiGate via 'show system admin'; cross-reference NewAdmin against the change-management ticket queue for the time window. Validate the originating admin's source IP against known jump hosts or admin VPN egress. Step 2 — Contain: if NewAdmin is not in the approved list, immediately delete the account ('config system admin / delete <NewAdmin>'), terminate all admin sessions, rotate all FortiGate admin credentials using PBKDF2 hashing (per CISA guidance), and snapshot the running config for forensics before any further changes. Step 3 — Hunt: review the FortiGate config diff (compare running-config to last-known-good) for other persistence changes — new API users, modified trusted hosts, new local certificates, modified SSL VPN portal settings, or added remote-syslog endpoints exfiltrating logs. Pivot the originating Admin source IP across other FortiGates in the estate for the same pattern.
let Window = 10m;
let AnomalousAdminAuth = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
    | where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
    | where Activity has_any ("Admin login successful","admin login success") or DeviceEventClassID == "0100032001"
    | project AuthTime = TimeGenerated, Admin = SourceUserName, AdminSrcIP = SourceIP, Firewall = DeviceName;
let AdminAccountChange = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
    | where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
    | where Activity has_any ("Edit system admin","Add system admin","config system admin","create admin")
         or DeviceEventClassID in ("0100041000","0100041001","0100041002")
    | project ChangeTime = TimeGenerated, ChangeBy = SourceUserName, ChangeSrcIP = SourceIP, Firewall = DeviceName, NewAdmin = DestinationHostName, ChangeMsg = Message;
AnomalousAdminAuth
| join kind=inner AdminAccountChange on $left.Admin == $right.ChangeBy, $left.Firewall == $right.Firewall
| where ChangeTime between (AuthTime .. AuthTime + Window)
| project AuthTime, ChangeTime, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', ChangeTime, AuthTime), Admin, AdminSrcIP, Firewall, NewAdmin, ChangeMsg
| order by AuthTime desc
source:fortinet (@evt.name:("Edit system admin" OR "Add system admin" OR "create admin") OR @msg:(*"config system admin"* OR *"Add system admin"*))
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(Authentication.src) as adminSrc, min(_time) as authTime from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app="fortigate-admin" Authentication.action="success" by Authentication.user, Authentication.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | rename user as admin, dest as firewall | join type=inner admin firewall [| tstats `summariesonly` min(_time) as adminAddTime, values(All_Changes.object) as newAdmins from datamodel=Change where Change.action IN ("created","modified") Change.object_category="firewall_admin" by Change.user, Change.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Change)` | rename user as admin, dest as firewall] | where adminAddTime > authTime AND adminAddTime < authTime + 600
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(Authentication.src) as adminSrc, min(_time) as authTime from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app="fortigate-admin" Authentication.action="success" by Authentication.user, Authentication.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | rename user as admin, dest as firewall | join type=inner admin firewall [| tstats summariesonly=false min(_time) as adminAddTime, values(All_Changes.object) as newAdmins from datamodel=Change where Change.action IN ("created","modified") Change.object_category="firewall_admin" by Change.user, Change.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Change)` | rename user as admin, dest as firewall] | where adminAddTime > authTime AND adminAddTime < authTime + 600
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")

     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

| where Account !endswith "$"

   or ParentProcessName endswith "\excel.exe"

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")

AutoJack: How a single page can RCE the host running your AI agent

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-06-19 7 use cases 7 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

AutoJack is a novel exploit chain showing how a single malicious webpage can turn an AI browsing agent into a remote code execution vector on the host machine. By abusing trust in localhost, missing authentication, and unsafe parameter handling, attackers can trigger arbitrary process execution through AutoGen Studio’s MCP WebSocket. The research highlights a broader pattern - when agents can browse untrusted content and access local services, traditional boundaries like localhost are no longer secure. The post AutoJack: How a single page can RCE the host running your AI agent appeared first o…

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] AutoJack: malicious WebSocket request to AutoGen Studio /api/mcp/ws/ with server_params query
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] AutoJack: AutoGen Studio backend spawns unexpected shell via StdioServerParams abuse · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — AutoJack: How a single page can RCE the host running your AI agent

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

AutoJack: AutoGen Studio backend spawns unexpected shell via StdioServerParams abuse AIExploitation High
Detects the AutoJack RCE primitive — the AutoGen Studio Python backend spawning a shell, LOLBin, or other arbitrary binary as a child process. Legitimate MCP servers launched via stdio are typically node/npx/python/uvx, so an autogenstudio parent spawning cmd/powershell/calc/bash/mshta/regsvr32 strongly implies the StdioServerParams (server_params query param) abuse described in the article. Rationale: Anchors on the article's specific exploitation footprint: the AutoGen Studio backend (Python process with 'autogenstudio' in its cmdline — the package is invoked as `autogenstudio ui` / `python -m autogenstudio.web`) spawning a child binary that doesn't fit a normal stdio MCP server runtime. The list of children is taken from the article's example payloads (calc.exe, powershell.exe -enc, bash -c) plus standard LOLBin extension. Cross-checked with the autogen GitHub repo confirming StdioServerParams is the canonical MCP stdio class. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/microsoft/autogen • https://microsoft.github.io/autogen/stable//reference/python/autogen_ext.tools.mcp.html
ATT&CKT1059 T1190 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer manually configures cmd.exe or powershell.exe as a stdio MCP server command for prototyping/testing
  • Legitimate MCP server wrapped in `cmd.exe /c <real-server>` for env-var expansion
  • Custom in-house MCP server implemented as a PowerShell script invoked via pwsh.exe
  • AutoGen Studio internal integration test that intentionally spawns calc.exe as a smoke test
  • Red-team / security validation of the AutoJack fix on a non-PyPI build
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("smoke-test","autogen-mcp-test","integration_test") or InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("buildagent","ci-runner"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the full process tree — confirm InitiatingProcessCommandLine actually contains 'autogenstudio' (vs incidental match) and inspect the child ProcessCommandLine for base64 strings, IEX, DownloadString, or network primitives that would indicate weaponisation. Pivot on the user/host to see if this is a known developer machine running AutoGen Studio. Step 2 (contain): If the cmdline shows weaponised content, kill the autogenstudio process tree, isolate the host via Defender Live Response, and rotate any credentials/tokens cached in the developer's profile (AAD refresh, Git PATs, AWS access keys). Step 3 (hunt): Pivot DeviceNetworkEvents on the same DeviceId for the prior 60 minutes to find the attacker page the agent rendered; check DeviceFileEvents for any payload dropped by the spawned shell; verify the AutoGen Studio install version against fix commit b047730.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("autogenstudio", "autogen_studio", "autogenstudio.web")
| where FileName in~ ("calc.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","wsl.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","msbuild.exe","installutil.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256, ProcessId
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("autogenstudio", "autogen_studio", "autogenstudio.web")
| where TargetProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\(calc|cmd|powershell|pwsh|bash|sh|wsl|mshta|rundll32|regsvr32|certutil|bitsadmin|curl|wget|wscript|cscript|msbuild|installutil)\.exe$"
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentCmd = ParentProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = TargetProcessName,
          ChildCmd   = TargetProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: AutoGen Studio Backend Spawns Suspicious Non-MCP Child Process (AutoJack)
id: 8c5d4b21-7e93-4f9a-9d56-a3b1c8e2f047
status: experimental
description: Detects the AutoJack exploit pattern where the AutoGen Studio Python backend spawns an arbitrary binary via StdioServerParams abuse on /api/mcp/ws/. Legitimate MCP servers typically run via node/npx/python/uvx, not shells or LOLBins.
references:
  - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/18/autojack-single-page-rce-host-running-ai-agent/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/19
tags:

  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1203

  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentCommandLine|contains:
      - 'autogenstudio'
      - 'autogen_studio'
      - 'autogenstudio.web'
  selection_child:

      - '\calc.exe'

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentCommandLine=/autogenstudio|autogen_studio/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(calc|cmd|powershell|pwsh|bash|sh|wsl|mshta|rundll32|regsvr32|certutil|bitsadmin|curl|wget|wscript|cscript|msbuild|installutil)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.process_path) as image values(Processes.process_hash) as sha256 from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process="*autogenstudio*" OR Processes.parent_process="*autogen_studio*" OR Processes.parent_process="*autogenstudio.web*") (Processes.process_name IN ("calc.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","wsl.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","msbuild.exe","installutil.exe")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.process_path) as image values(Processes.process_hash) as sha256 from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process="*autogenstudio*" OR Processes.parent_process="*autogen_studio*" OR Processes.parent_process="*autogenstudio.web*") (Processes.process_name IN ("calc.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","wsl.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","msbuild.exe","installutil.exe")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
AutoJack: malicious WebSocket request to AutoGen Studio /api/mcp/ws/ with server_params query AIDelivery High
Detects the AutoJack network footprint — an HTTP/WebSocket request to the AutoGen Studio MCP control plane (/api/mcp/ws/) carrying a base64-encoded server_params query parameter. This is the exact pre-RCE signature: the agent's headless browser (or any client) issuing the WebSocket upgrade that smuggles the StdioServerParams payload past the origin allowlist and unauth'd /api/mcp/* path. Rationale: Path /api/mcp/ws/ + query parameter name server_params are verbatim from the article's WebSocket route definition (code block 2) and exploit URL example ('ws://localhost:8081/api/mcp/ws/?server_params='). Both strings co-occurring is essentially zero-FP unless someone is testing the patched build. The Falcon variant pivots on the article-named port 8081 + the agent's browser process making the connection. Cross-checked AutoGen autogen_ext.tools.mcp module which confirms StdioServerParams shape. Cross-checked against: • https://microsoft.github.io/autogen/stable//_modules/autogen_ext/tools/mcp/_stdio.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1659
Data sourcesWeb.web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorised red-team validation of AutoJack fix on dev builds
  • AutoGen maintainer regression tests hitting the endpoint
  • Security researcher reproducing CVE on an isolated lab host
  • Legitimate developer manually crafting a WebSocket call to test their own MCP server registration flow
  • Internal vulnerability scanner (Tenable/Qualys) issuing a probe against /api/mcp/ws/
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("tenable.exe","nessusd.exe","qualys-cs.exe","nuclei.exe") or RemoteUrl has "X-Pentest-Auth=")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Decode the base64 server_params value from the URL (or pull it from the request log) and inspect the StdioServerParams JSON — the `command` and `args` fields reveal attacker intent (calc.exe = demo, anything else = real). Identify the source IP and the AutoGen Studio host. Step 2 (contain): Block the source IP at the perimeter, stop the autogenstudio service on the target host, and snapshot memory before reboot — the spawned child may still be live. Step 3 (hunt): Correlate to UC1 process tree to confirm execution actually occurred; check for outbound C2 from any child the spawned binary created; verify upstream AutoGen Studio version is at or past commit b047730. Audit any other MCP-WebSocket or local-control-plane services on the same host for the same loopback-trust pattern.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "/api/mcp/ws/" and RemoteUrl has "server_params="
| project Timestamp, DeviceName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where Url has "/api/mcp/ws/" and Url has "server_params="
    | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, Url, HttpMethod, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent),
  (W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where csUriStem has "/api/mcp/ws/" and csUriQuery has "server_params="
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csUserAgent, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:

        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote

      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

2026-06-18 9 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The Gentlemen ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) is actively developing and maintaining a suite of endpoint detection and response (EDR) killers to help affiliates evade detection in attacks. [...]

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Themida/Enigma packed binary with security-vendor masquerade name from user-writable path
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] GentleKiller / HexKiller / ThrottleBlood / HavocKiller binary hash hit · [LLM] BYOVD vulnerable-driver service install impersonating Kaspersky/Valorant/Javelin/WatchDog · [LLM] Mass termination of 48-vendor EDR/AV process set within short window · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
GentleKiller / HexKiller / ThrottleBlood / HavocKiller binary hash hit AIInstallation High
Alerts on execution or file-write of any binary whose SHA1 matches the 20 ESET-published GentleKiller/HexKiller/ThrottleBlood/HavocKiller hashes tied to Gentlemen RaaS. These hashes were enumerated by ESET across at least 8 GentleKiller variants and three external EDR-killers. A hit means an in-scope ransomware-precursor binary touched the host and pre-encryption defense-disablement is imminent. Rationale: Uses the 20 SHA1 hashes attributed by ESET (the only researchers cited) to GentleKiller/HexKiller/ThrottleBlood/HavocKiller, covering both execution (ProcessEvents) and on-disk drop (FileEvents). The hash list is the article's most concrete IOC set and the only one that gives an unambiguous true-positive verdict.
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Reverse-engineer or malware analyst intentionally detonating sample on a lab host
  • SOC purple-team or BAS tool replaying the same hashes in a controlled test
  • Threat-intel ingestion pipeline writing the binary to a hashed quarantine path
  • Backup or forensic-imaging tools copying a previously-detected sample
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("malware-lab","sandbox-","-detonation") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\AVAnalysis\", @"\Forensics\"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE — confirm the device is a production endpoint, not the malware-analysis lab; pull full ProcessEvents/FileEvents tree for the matching SHA1 in the prior 60 minutes; identify the initiating user and parent binary (typical Gentlemen chain has the killer dropped after initial RDP / RMM intrusion). 2) CONTAIN — isolate the host via Defender or Falcon network containment; expire all cached credentials for the logged-on user; query EDR for any service stops on security products (Defender/CrowdStrike/SentinelOne) in the last 24h on this host. 3) HUNT — pivot on the parent process hash and the dropping account across the fleet; query for the same hashes anywhere in the estate (file-events) and for vulnerable-driver names (see UC2) since Gentlemen affiliates often pre-stage drivers on multiple hosts before encryption.
let GentlemenSHA1 = dynamic(["8AE6BD18B129061F63642531F1B684CF0383C75D","BA914FE77B177B45799403B16DD14765C510A074","D605994FC72A2BB59B5CFB1624A1B9170ECA73A2","B0B912A3FD1C05D72080848EC4C92880004021A1","5AA3124E5C4921E5EDFC60133B5D71DA21B07DA3","7556AE58C215B8245A43F764F0676C7A8F0FDD1A","331879F5EEC8892BBD896F90BDBB1BAD0BF63BD6","F11AEBCCB9A86A7E2E653F90BAEC697F233C255F","EF9CD06683159397F099CAA244E94E6EAAD96EBA","711EF221526997039E804A18DB9647C91680BBE2","68FEC379F2AE76C3D2CE913F7BE650CEA1D06990","A11EE9CDC59E5CAA59AEFD27B30D104F3AD68E62","96F0DBF52AED0AFD43E44500116B04B674F7358E","2F86898528C6CAB3540C486A9BFAA0C029B73950","9AD51AD97C01E97AB59214116740785E0F6320A8","A19117175DBC9BA4D23B5DCE8415E299A2E32192","12500F6C87CE62712A0ED6652C57468D15C14223","D29670E684E40DDC89B47010C37CBC96737035B6","56BEE9DF5833A637F5C54D5911DF98B0812FE643","CF4D74DF17A91B4A36A2911B22AFEC5D8FA93A01"]);
let ProcHits = DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where SHA1 in~ (GentlemenSHA1) or InitiatingProcessSHA1 in~ (GentlemenSHA1)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
let FileHits = DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where SHA1 in~ (GentlemenSHA1) or InitiatingProcessSHA1 in~ (GentlemenSHA1)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName=FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
ProcHits | union FileHits | order by Timestamp desc

BYOVD vulnerable-driver service install impersonating Kaspersky/Valorant/Javelin/WatchDog AIInstallation Medium
Hunts kernel-driver service creation where the service or ImagePath uses names GentleKiller variants impersonate — Kaspersky, Valorant (Riot), Javelin, WatchDog — but the driver file does NOT live under the legitimate vendor path. Catches the BYOVD step where Gentlemen registers a vulnerable driver under a security-product mask to obtain Ring 0. Rationale: Article explicitly lists Kaspersky / Valorant / Javelin / WatchDog as the four product names that GentleKiller variants impersonate, and ESET notes each variant ships a different vulnerable driver. Detecting the impersonated service-name + non-vendor path catches the BYOVD step regardless of which CVE driver the affiliate loads.
ATT&CKT1068 T1543.003 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Kaspersky AV reinstall from a non-standard custom installer path
  • Legit Valorant/Vanguard install on a corporate dev host (rare but happens on dual-use laptops)
  • Security-vendor IR tooling that registers a temporary kernel helper under a vendor-branded service name
  • Pen-test or BAS tool simulating a BYOVD install
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("explorer.exe") and InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$" and RegistryValueData has_any (@"\Kaspersky Lab\", @"\Riot Vanguard\"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE — pull the InitiatingProcess (who registered the service) and the driver file SHA256; cross-reference the SHA256 against loldrivers.io to confirm it is a known vulnerable driver; verify the legit vendor product is/isn't actually installed via DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory. 2) CONTAIN — stop and delete the rogue service (sc.exe delete <name>) before reboot; isolate the host; revoke the user session that wrote the registry value. 3) HUNT — pivot on the writing process across the fleet; search DeviceFileEvents for the driver SHA256 on every endpoint (Gentlemen pre-stages drivers across multiple hosts); check for any of the 20 hashes in UC1 on the same host in the prior 24h.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\"
| where (RegistryValueName =~ "ImagePath" and RegistryValueData has_any ("kaspersky","valorant","vgk.sys","javelin","watchdog","wdog","wsdk"))
     or (RegistryKey has_any (@"\Services\kaspersky",@"\Services\valorant",@"\Services\vgk",@"\Services\javelin",@"\Services\watchdog",@"\Services\wdog") and RegistryValueName =~ "ImagePath")
| where not (RegistryValueData has_any (@"\Program Files\Kaspersky Lab\", @"\Program Files\Riot Vanguard\", @"\Program Files\Valorant\"))
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA1
| order by Timestamp desc
let ImpersonatedNames = dynamic(["kaspersky","valorant","vgk","javelin","watchdog","wdog","wsdk"]);
let LegitPaths = dynamic([@"\Program Files\Kaspersky Lab\", @"\Program Files\Riot Vanguard\", @"\Program Files\Valorant\"]);
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Source == "Service Control Manager" and EventID == 7045
| extend ServiceName = tostring(parse_xml(EventData).EventData.Data[0])
| extend ImagePath = tostring(parse_xml(EventData).EventData.Data[1])
| extend ServiceType = tostring(parse_xml(EventData).EventData.Data[2])
| where ServiceType has "kernel" or ImagePath endswith ".sys"
| where tolower(ServiceName) has_any (ImpersonatedNames) or tolower(ImagePath) has_any (ImpersonatedNames)
| where not (ImagePath has_any (LegitPaths))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ServiceName, ImagePath, ServiceType, User
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Gentlemen RaaS BYOVD Driver Service Install Impersonating Security Vendor
id: 7f1b6f08-d34a-4f3b-9d22-3a5e7c1c9a02
description: Detects creation of a kernel-mode service whose name or ImagePath impersonates Kaspersky, Riot Vanguard (Valorant/vgk), Javelin or WatchDog — the GentleKiller BYOVD masquerade — when the driver does not reside under the legitimate vendor path.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/gentlemen-ransomware-uses-multiple-edr-killers-to-disable-defenses/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/19
tags:
  - attack.t1068
  - attack.t1543.003
  - attack.t1036.005
