Scheduled task registers wscript/cscript-launched payload for clipper persistence AIInstallation High
Detects the worm component installing scheduled-task persistence for itself and the clipper, as described in the article. Looks for schtasks.exe creating tasks whose action invokes wscript.exe or cscript.exe with a user-writable path (Temp, AppData, ProgramData, Public). Rationale: Article: 'The worm component … deploys scheduled tasks as a form of persistence for both the worm component and the stealer component.' The clipper uses WScript/ActiveXObject so any installed task action will reference wscript or cscript pointing at a payload outside Program Files — that combination is rarely benign.
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1547
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate enterprise login-banner script deployed via scheduled task pointing to ProgramData
  • Software-vendor uninstaller cleanup tasks shipping VBS in %ProgramData%\<Vendor>\
  • Adobe/Java updater registered as scheduled-task VBS hooks
  • IT-admin ad-hoc tasks running diagnostic VBS from a user profile path
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\System32\\CCM\\" and ProcessCommandLine !has "\\Program Files\\"
Response runbook
Triage: extract task name and the full TR (task-run) argument from the command line; pull the referenced script for sandbox analysis. Contain: delete the scheduled task with schtasks /Delete /F, kill any running instances, and isolate the host. Hunt: query DeviceEvents for ActionType=ScheduledTaskCreated across the fleet for the same script SHA256 or task name, and check DeviceFileEvents for the original payload file to identify the delivery vector (USB drive letter or download URL).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/Create","/CREATE")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("wscript","cscript")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\AppData\\","\\Temp\\","\\ProgramData\\","\\Public\\","\\Users\\Public\\")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("/Create","/CREATE")
| where CommandLine has_any ("wscript","cscript")
| where CommandLine has_any ("\\AppData\\","\\Temp\\","\\ProgramData\\","\\Public\\","\\Users\\Public\\")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Schtasks Registers WScript Or CScript Payload From User-Writable Path
id: 5f2b9c41-7d18-4a93-91be-3e95ad6c4d22
description: Detects schtasks.exe creating a scheduled task whose action invokes wscript.exe or cscript.exe against a payload in a user-writable directory, matching the Microsoft-reported clipper persistence step.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/microsoft-details-windows-clipper.html
author: thn-usecases
date: 2026/06/18
tags:
  - attack.t1053.005
  - attack.t1547
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\schtasks.exe'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '/Create'
      - '/CREATE'
  script_engine:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'wscript'
      - 'cscript'
  user_writable:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '\AppData\'
      - '\Temp\'
      - '\ProgramData\'
      - '\Public\'
      - '\Users\Public\'
  condition: selection and script_engine and user_writable
level: high
source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.security) (@EventID:1 OR @EventID:4688) @Image:(*\\schtasks.exe OR *\\SCHTASKS.EXE) @CommandLine:((*Create* OR *CREATE*) AND (*wscript* OR *cscript* OR *WScript* OR *CScript*) AND (*AppData* OR *Temp* OR *ProgramData* OR *Public*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/schtasks\.exe$/i
| regex("(?i)/create", field=CommandLine)
| regex("(?i)(wscript|cscript)", field=CommandLine)
| regex("(?i)\\\\(AppData|Temp|ProgramData|Public|Users\\\\Public)\\\\", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=schtasks.exe (Processes.process="*/Create*" OR Processes.process="* /CREATE *") (Processes.process="*wscript*" OR Processes.process="*cscript*") (Processes.process="*\\AppData\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\Temp\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\ProgramData\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\Public\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\Users\\Public\\*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=schtasks.exe (Processes.process="*/Create*" OR Processes.process="* /CREATE *") (Processes.process="*wscript*" OR Processes.process="*cscript*") (Processes.process="*\\AppData\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\Temp\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\ProgramData\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\Public\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\Users\\Public\\*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Local SOCKS5 listener on Tor-default port from non-browser binary (bundled Tor proxy) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the bundled Tor client described in the article: a renamed Tor binary opening a local SOCKS5 listener on the default Tor ports (9050/9150) from a process that is not Tor Browser, Brave, or another known Tor-aware app. The clipper routes C2 through this local proxy, so the listener is a strong signal. Rationale: Article states the malware 'launches a renamed Tor binary in a hidden window' and 'routes traffic through a local SOCKS5 proxy.' Tor's default SOCKS5 ports are 9050 (tor.exe) and 9150 (Tor Browser). A loopback connection or listener on those ports from a process that is NOT a known Tor client is exactly the renamed-Tor signature the article describes.
ATT&CKT1090.003 T1572 T1036.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer using Tor SOCKS proxy via a custom Python script for legitimate research
  • Privacy-tool users running Tor via OnionShare or BridgeRelay portables under a renamed wrapper
  • Penetration-tester using torsocks during an authorised engagement
  • Anonymisation-aware crypto wallet apps (e.g. Wasabi, Samourai) that ship their own SOCKS5 binding
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\Tor Browser\\" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\OnionShare\\"
Response runbook
Triage: identify the binding process via InitiatingProcessSHA256 and InitiatingProcessFolderPath; submit hash to threat intel and inspect the on-disk binary for Tor strings/imports despite the renamed filename. Contain: kill the proxy process, isolate the host, capture memory if possible, then quarantine the binary. Hunt: query DeviceProcessEvents for the same SHA256 across the fleet, check DeviceRegistryEvents and scheduled-task creations referencing the same path, and look at DeviceFileEvents for any .onion-related config files (torrc) dropped to %AppData% or %ProgramData%.
let TorPorts = dynamic([9050, 9150]);
let KnownTorClients = dynamic(["tor.exe","firefox.exe","tor-browser.exe","brave.exe","torbrowser.exe"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt","ListeningConnectionCreated")
| where RemotePort in (TorPorts) or LocalPort in (TorPorts)
| where RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1","::1") or LocalIP in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ (KnownTorClients)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256,
          LocalIP, LocalPort, RemoteIP, RemotePort, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
let TorPorts = dynamic([9050, 9150]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstPortNumber in (TorPorts) or SrcPortNumber in (TorPorts)
| where DstIpAddr in ("127.0.0.1","::1") or SrcIpAddr in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcPortNumber, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 (@DestinationPort:9050 OR @DestinationPort:9150) @DestinationIp:(127.0.0.1 OR \:\:1) -@Image:(*\\tor.exe OR *\\Tor.exe OR *\\TOR.EXE OR *\\firefox.exe OR *\\Firefox.exe OR *\\tor-browser.exe OR *\\brave.exe OR *\\Brave.exe)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 (RemotePort=9050 OR RemotePort=9150) RemoteAddressIP4=/^127\./
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/(tor|firefox|tor-browser|torbrowser|brave)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemotePort], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest_port=9050 OR All_Traffic.dest_port=9150) (All_Traffic.dest_ip="127.0.0.1" OR All_Traffic.dest_ip="::1") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app All_Traffic.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where NOT (process_name IN ("tor.exe","firefox.exe","tor-browser.exe","brave.exe"))
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest_port=9050 OR All_Traffic.dest_port=9150) (All_Traffic.dest_ip="127.0.0.1" OR All_Traffic.dest_ip="::1") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app All_Traffic.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where NOT (process_name IN ("tor.exe","firefox.exe","tor-browser.exe","brave.exe"))
PowerShell screen capture via System.Drawing CopyFromScreen (Microsoft clipper signal) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the clipper's screenshot-exfiltration stage. Microsoft's article explicitly recommends 'PowerShell-based screen capture' detection. The Bitmap/Graphics/CopyFromScreen API pattern is the canonical way PowerShell grabs the desktop and is rarely seen in benign workloads. Rationale: Direct Microsoft recommendation in the article: 'defenders prioritize behavioral detections … specifically looking for PowerShell-based screen capture.' The .NET System.Drawing classes with CopyFromScreen are the standard PowerShell screenshot pattern and the clipper does periodic screen-grab exfiltration over Tor — so the API string is the natural cmd-line fingerprint.
ATT&CKT1113 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal ITAM or RMM tool grabbing screenshots for endpoint inventory dashboards
  • Developer testing a screenshot-utility PowerShell module
  • Help-desk session-recording scripts using Bitmap APIs for incident capture
  • ScreenConnect/ConnectWise remote-support agents using PowerShell wrappers for thumbnails
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\ScreenConnect\\" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\ConnectWise\\" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\SCCM\\"
Response runbook
Triage: extract the full PowerShell command line, decode any inline base64 or compressed payload, identify the target output path (where the bitmap is written). Contain: kill the PowerShell process tree, isolate the host, and review %TEMP%/%APPDATA% for recently-written PNG/JPG/BMP files that may be queued for Tor upload. Hunt: pivot on InitiatingProcessFileName — if wscript.exe or cscript.exe is the parent, this is the clipper chain; query DeviceNetworkEvents for the parent process touching localhost:9050/9150 and pull any scheduled tasks that launch the same script.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("System.Drawing","CopyFromScreen","Drawing.Bitmap","Drawing.Graphics","FromImage","PrimaryScreen.Bounds")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any ("System.Drawing","CopyFromScreen","Drawing.Bitmap","Drawing.Graphics","FromImage","PrimaryScreen.Bounds")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |

references:

Vulnerable praisonai-platform server launch (GHSA-f38v-77qj-h4jq / CVE-2026-47410) AIInstallation High
Detects Python/uvicorn launching the praisonai-platform FastAPI app, the documented entry points 'python -m praisonai_platform' and 'uvicorn praisonai_platform.api.app:app'. Versions <=0.1.4 sign/verify JWTs with the public literal 'dev-secret-change-me' whenever PLATFORM_JWT_SECRET is unset and PLATFORM_ENV defaults to 'dev', which is the unmodified default state of the package. Identifies exposed vulnerable instances before exploitation. Rationale: Article names the exact documented entry points: 'python -m praisonai_platform --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000' and 'uvicorn praisonai_platform.api.app:app --host 0.0.0.0' (auth_service.py path src/praisonai-platform/praisonai_platform/services/auth_service.py). Detecting these launches identifies vulnerable deployments since 0.1.4 == default-open. Cross-checked parent advisory GHSA-3qg8-5g3r-79v5 / CVE-2026-47410 confirming the hardcoded secret 'dev-secret-change-me' and that no shipped Dockerfile / compose sets PLATFORM_JWT_SECRET. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3qg8-5g3r-79v5 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/praisonai-platform/CVE-2026-47410/ • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-3qg8-5g3r-79v5
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running the server locally with PLATFORM_JWT_SECRET and PLATFORM_ENV=prod explicitly exported
  • CI/CD integration-test runner that spins up the package in an ephemeral container
  • QA staging host that is firewall-isolated from the public internet
  • Security researcher reproducing the PoC in a sandbox
  • Internal documentation/training environment
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !has_any ("dev-", "staging-", "ci-", "build-", "qa-") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "PLATFORM_JWT_SECRET="
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the host owner and confirm whether the instance is dev/test (allow-listed) or production-exposed. On the running PID, read `tr '\0' '\n' < /proc/<pid>/environ` and verify PLATFORM_JWT_SECRET is set to a strong random value (NOT 'dev-secret-change-me') AND PLATFORM_ENV != 'dev'. Step 2 (contain): If unset or default, export a fresh 32+ byte random PLATFORM_JWT_SECRET and restart — this invalidates every existing JWT (legit and forged). If internet-exposed, place behind authenticating reverse proxy or take offline until rotated; consider pinning a patched fork. Step 3 (hunt): Pull web-access logs for the host's listening port over the last 30 days for any DELETE on /workspaces/{uuid} or GET on /{uuid}/members and the source IPs/UAs; correlate against pre-rotation JWT subs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3","python3.exe","python","uvicorn","uvicorn.exe","gunicorn") or FileName in~ ("python.exe","python3","python3.exe","python","uvicorn","uvicorn.exe","gunicorn")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai_platform.api.app:app", "-m praisonai_platform", "praisonai_platform --host")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai_platform.api.app:app", "-m praisonai_platform", "praisonai_platform --host")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("python","python3","uvicorn","gunicorn")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Vulnerable praisonai-platform Server Launch (GHSA-f38v-77qj-h4jq / CVE-2026-47410)

description: |
  Detects launch of the praisonai-platform FastAPI server. Versions <=0.1.4 sign and verify
  JWTs with the public default secret 'dev-secret-change-me' unless PLATFORM_JWT_SECRET is set

praisonai-platform workspace-member enumeration fan-out (forged-JWT recon) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for a single source IP or principal reading GET /{workspace_id}/members across many distinct workspaces in a short window. Per the article, this endpoint returns every member's user_id, which an attacker holding a forged JWT uses to identify workspace-owner user_ids before targeted owner impersonation. Threshold-based behavioural detection. Rationale: Article explicitly identifies GET /{workspace_id}/members as the discovery primitive that reveals workspace-owner user_ids ('returns List[MemberResponse], each carrying user_id and role, to any holder of require_workspace_member'). user_ids are uuid4 per the article so the UUID regex on the path component is tight. Fan-out (>=5 distinct workspaces from one src) is the high-fidelity signal — legit members read one workspace's members; attackers iterate. defender_kql empty: web access logs are not in Defender XDR tables. falcon_logscale_query empty: Falcon FDR does not ship HTTP URL paths from arbitrary applications. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3qg8-5g3r-79v5
ATT&CKT1087.004 T1213
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Workspace admin auditing members across many workspaces they own
  • Compliance/backup tool that periodically enumerates members for export
  • E2E test suite that creates many workspaces then lists their members
  • SSO provisioning sync agent reconciling membership
  • Customer-success rep helping users across many workspaces
Suppression filter
| where csUserName !in~ ("svc-praison-compliance", "svc-praison-backup", "svc-praison-provisioning") and csUserAgent !has_any ("praison-backup-agent", "compliance-scanner/")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Resolve cIP and csUserName to a human or service principal; check whether they legitimately own/admin the enumerated workspaces. Confirm the JWT 'sub' from the X-Authenticated-User / app log matches the expected csUserName. Step 2 (contain): If the principal isn't an authorised admin, immediately rotate PLATFORM_JWT_SECRET (invalidates all sessions), force re-auth, and block the source IP. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to DELETE actions on /workspaces/{id} or PATCH/PUT on /{id}/members/{user_id} from the same cIP / csUserName over the last 7d; check for newly-created admin members; look for the same fan-out pattern from other sources.
let UuidRe = @"^/[0-9a-fA-F]{8}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{12}/members$";
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where csMethod == "GET"
| where csUriStem matches regex UuidRe
| summarize WorkspacesEnumerated = dcount(csUriStem),
            FirstHit = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastHit  = max(TimeGenerated),
            SampleAgent = any(csUserAgent),
            SampleStatus = any(scStatus),
            SampleWorkspaces = make_set(csUriStem, 10)
            by cIP, csUserName
| where WorkspacesEnumerated >= 5
| order by WorkspacesEnumerated desc
(source:nginx OR source:apache OR source:aws.alb) @http.method:GET @http.url_details.path:*/members
# log group: /aws/applicationelb (point at the ALB fronting praisonai-platform)
fields @timestamp, client.ip, request, elb_status_code, user_agent
| filter request like /GET https?:\/\/[^\/]+\/[0-9a-fA-F]{8}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{12}\/members/
| stats count_distinct(request) as workspaces_enumerated, min(@timestamp) as first_seen, max(@timestamp) as last_seen by client.ip
| filter workspaces_enumerated >= 5
| sort workspaces_enumerated desc

| tstats summariesonly=false dc(Web.url) as workspaces_enumerated, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime, values(Web.user_agent) as user_agents, values(Web.url) as sample_urls from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.http_method="GET" Web.url="*/members" Web.url="*-*-*-*-*/members" by Web.src Web.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where workspaces_enumerated >= 5 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
praisonai-platform workspace / member destructive DELETE (forged-JWT impact) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects DELETE requests on praisonai-platform's owner-gated destructive endpoints: DELETE /workspaces/{workspace_id} (wipes the workspace + every contained resource) and DELETE /{workspace_id}/members/{user_id} (evicts legitimate members). Per the article these are the irrecoverable A:H operations reachable via a forged JWT signed with the public default secret. Rationale: Article calls out the exact destructive routes: 'DELETE /workspaces/{workspace_id} (gated by require_workspace_owner), which deletes the entire workspace and every contained resource, and DELETE /{workspace_id}/members/{user_id}, which evicts legitimate members'. Both gated only by JWT 'sub' matching workspace_owner role, which the forged token satisfies. uuid4 path components yield tight regex anchors. Cross-checked sibling advisories GHSA-c2m8-4gcg-v22g (9.6) and GHSA-h8q5-cp56-rr65 (referenced) confirming the same routes. defender_kql empty: HTTP access logs are not in Defender XDR. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3qg8-5g3r-79v5 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/praisonai-platform/CVE-2026-47410/
ATT&CKT1485 T1531 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate workspace owner deleting their own old/test workspace
  • Admin offboarding script evicting departed employees from member lists
  • E2E test teardown that creates and then deletes ephemeral workspaces
  • Customer-initiated account closure flow that cascades workspace delete
  • Bulk-cleanup job removing workspaces flagged for end-of-life
Suppression filter
| where csUserName !in~ ("svc-praison-admin", "svc-praison-offboarding") and not (csUserAgent has_any ("praison-e2e", "praison-cleanup-job") and sSiteName has_any ("staging", "test"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Snapshot the request — cIP, csUserName/JWT sub, scStatus, csUserAgent. Confirm with the workspace owner out-of-band whether they actually initiated the DELETE (if 2xx, the resource is already gone). Verify the deployment's PLATFORM_JWT_SECRET is not the default 'dev-secret-change-me'. Step 2 (contain): If unauthorised or the secret is default, immediately rotate PLATFORM_JWT_SECRET to a strong random value (invalidates all forged AND legit tokens — accept the user-impact tradeoff), force re-auth, block the source IP at WAF. Restore the workspace from the most recent backup. Step 3 (hunt): Enumerate all DELETE/PATCH on /workspaces/* and /*/members/* over the prior 30 days; correlate by source IP, csUserName, and JWT sub; check for orphaned workspaces that lost their owner; review GHSA-c2m8-4gcg-v22g and GHSA-h8q5-cp56-rr65 for related privilege paths.
let WorkspaceDel = @"^/workspaces/[0-9a-fA-F]{8}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{12}$";
let MemberDel    = @"^/[0-9a-fA-F]{8}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{12}/members/[0-9a-fA-F]{8}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{12}$";
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where csMethod == "DELETE"
| where csUriStem matches regex WorkspaceDel
   or  csUriStem matches regex MemberDel
| where scStatus startswith "2"          // succeeded
| project TimeGenerated, cIP, csUserName, csMethod, csUriStem, scStatus, csUserAgent, sSiteName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Vulnerable PraisonAI package exposure (< 4.6.61, GHSA-29w3-p9w9-wc47)

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] PraisonAI multiedit tool reading sensitive credentials (GHSA-29w3-p9w9-wc47)
PraisonAI multiedit tool reading sensitive credentials (GHSA-29w3-p9w9-wc47) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts Python processes running PraisonAI (module 'praisonai.tools.multiedit') accessing files outside any reasonable workspace boundary — SSH private keys, AWS credentials, .env files, /etc/shadow. The multiedit tool's lack of path validation lets prompt-injected agents read arbitrary files via the dry_run diff output or direct read path. Rationale: Detection anchors on three article-specific tokens: (1) Python interpreter as initiating process, (2) 'praisonai' or 'multiedit' in command line (the vulnerable tool's module path is praisonai.tools.multiedit), (3) sensitive credential paths explicitly named in the article's Impact section (/etc/shadow, ~/.ssh/id_rsa, ~/.aws/credentials, .env). The combination is high-fidelity because no legitimate workspace-scoped agent should be traversing to /etc/ or user home credential stores.
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.004 T1083
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer explicitly asking PraisonAI agent to read or rotate their own ~/.aws/credentials in a personal lab environment
  • Legitimate PraisonAI workflow that ingests a project's .env file from inside the workspace (path will contain workspace root, not /root or $HOME)
  • Security researcher reproducing the GHSA-29w3-p9w9-wc47 PoC in a sandbox after the advisory landed
  • PraisonAI agent indexing a Git repository whose path happens to contain '.env.example' or similar template files
  • Automated dotfile sync tool spawned as a child of a PraisonAI orchestration session
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has "/workspace/" or FolderPath has "/app/data/")
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "pytest" and FolderPath has "/tests/fixtures/")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the deployment shape — CLI dev workstation vs chatbot integration (Telegram/Discord/Slack with auto_approve_tools=True is the high-risk path). Pull the agent's prompt/conversation log around the file-access timestamp; the prompt that drove the multiedit call is the smoking gun. Step 2 (contain): If the file accessed was a credential store, immediately rotate the secret (SSH key, AWS access key, .env API keys) and revoke active sessions. Pin or remove the multiedit tool from the agent's tool registry until upgraded to praisonai >= 4.6.61. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the same host for (a) outbound network connections from the Python process to non-corporate destinations in the 10 minutes following the read, (b) subsequent file WRITES by the same process to authorized_keys/.bashrc (see persistence UC), (c) other LLM agent tools in the org's stack with similar path-validation gaps.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
   or ActionType startswith "File"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe", "python3", "python", "python3.exe", "pythonw.exe", "python3.10", "python3.11", "python3.12")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai", "multiedit")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\.ssh\", @"\.aws\", @"\.env", @"\.netrc", "/etc/shadow", "/etc/passwd", "/.ssh/", "/.aws/", "/root/", "id_rsa", "id_ed25519", "credentials")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python", "python3", "pythonw")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai", "multiedit")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/.ssh/", "/.aws/", "/.env", "/.netrc", "/etc/shadow", "/etc/passwd", "id_rsa", "id_ed25519", "credentials", @"\.ssh\", @"\.aws\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: PraisonAI MultiEdit Tool Accessing Sensitive Credentials
id: 8b3f4e2a-91c7-4a5d-b8f1-3e9c5d2a7f64
description: Detects the PraisonAI Python agent (vulnerable multiedit tool, GHSA-29w3-p9w9-wc47) reading credentials, SSH keys, or cloud secrets outside any plausible workspace. The multiedit tool lacks path validation and traversal protection.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-29w3-p9w9-wc47
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/18
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1552.001
  - attack.t1552.004
logsource:
  product: linux
  category: file_event
detection:
  selection_proc:
    Image|contains: 'python'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'praisonai'
      - 'multiedit'
  selection_target:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '/.ssh/id_'
      - '/.aws/credentials'
      - '/.aws/config'
      - '/.env'
      - '/.netrc'
      - '/etc/shadow'
      - '/etc/passwd'
      - 'authorized_keys'
  condition: selection_proc and selection_target
falsepositives:
  - Developer explicitly invoking PraisonAI to manage their own credentials/SSH keys
  - Automated PraisonAI workflows that legitimately read .env config from a known workspace
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:(PATH OR SYSCALL) @process.name:(python OR python3 OR pythonw) @process.command_line:(*praisonai* OR *multiedit*) @file.path:(*/.ssh/id_* OR */.aws/credentials* OR */.env OR */.netrc OR /etc/shadow OR /etc/passwd OR *authorized_keys*)
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo
| ContextImageFileName=/python[3]?(w)?(\.exe)?$/i
| regex("(/\.ssh/id_|/\.aws/credentials|/\.aws/config|/\.env$|/\.netrc|/etc/shadow|/etc/passwd|authorized_keys|\\\\\.ssh\\\\|\\\\\.aws\\\\)", field=TargetFileName)
| join({
    #event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
    | regex("(praisonai|multiedit)", field=CommandLine)
  }, field=ContextProcessId, key=TargetProcessId, include=[CommandLine, ImageFileName])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.file_path) as file_paths from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.process_name="python*" OR Filesystem.process_name="python3*" OR Filesystem.process_name="pythonw.exe") AND (Filesystem.file_path="*/.ssh/id_rsa*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/.ssh/id_ed25519*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/.aws/credentials*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/.aws/config*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/etc/shadow" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/etc/passwd" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/.netrc" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/.env" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.ssh\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.aws\\credentials*") by host Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.process_id Filesystem.action Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | join type=inner host process_id [| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*praisonai*" OR Processes.process="*multiedit*") by host Processes.process_id Processes.process Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`] | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.file_path) as file_paths from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.process_name="python*" OR Filesystem.process_name="python3*" OR Filesystem.process_name="pythonw.exe") AND (Filesystem.file_path="*/.ssh/id_rsa*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/.ssh/id_ed25519*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/.aws/credentials*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/.aws/config*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/etc/shadow" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/etc/passwd" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/.netrc" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/.env" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.ssh\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.aws\\credentials*") by host Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.process_id Filesystem.action Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | join type=inner host process_id [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*praisonai*" OR Processes.process="*multiedit*") by host Processes.process_id Processes.process Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`] | sort - lastTime
PraisonAI multiedit writing to persistence locations (authorized_keys / shell rc / cron) AIInstallation High
Hunts the write-side abuse of the GHSA-29w3-p9w9-wc47 multiedit vulnerability — a Python PraisonAI process writing/modifying files in canonical Linux/Windows persistence locations (~/.ssh/authorized_keys, ~/.bashrc, ~/.bash_profile, ~/.profile, cron, autostart) where no workspace-scoped agent should ever touch. The advisory explicitly calls out writing to ~/.bashrc and ~/.ssh/authorized_keys as the privilege-escalation impact. Rationale: Anchors on the article's Impact section, which explicitly names ~/.bashrc and ~/.ssh/authorized_keys as the privilege-escalation outcomes. Combining the Python+praisonai/multiedit cmdline filter with these specific persistence paths makes this alerting-tier — there is essentially no legitimate scenario where a PraisonAI agent should rewrite a user's shell rc or SSH authorized_keys outside an explicit provisioning playbook.
ATT&CKT1098.004 T1546.004 T1053.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin using PraisonAI as a deliberate Ansible-style provisioner to push authorized_keys to fleet hosts
  • Developer asking PraisonAI to add an alias to their own .bashrc on a personal dev VM
  • Container/cloud-init bootstrap script that happens to embed PraisonAI for initial host config
  • Security researcher reproducing the PoC from the advisory
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "ansible" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "cloud-init")
| where not (DeviceName startswith "dev-" and AccountName == "developer")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Diff the modified file against backup/git history — the inserted content is the payload. Common shapes: a new SSH public key not matching any known engineer fingerprint, a curl|sh trampoline appended to .bashrc, an entry in cron.d calling out to an external URL. Pull the PraisonAI session/prompt that drove the write. Step 2 (contain): Revert the file from backup; if authorized_keys was modified, kill all live SSH sessions for that account and rotate any other access. Disable the agent integration (Telegram/Discord/Slack bot token, API key) and pin praisonai package to >= 4.6.61 across the fleet. Step 3 (hunt): Search 24h forward for SSH logins to this host from any IP whose pubkey matches the freshly-added one; search the org for other hosts where the same praisonai process wrote anywhere outside its workspace.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe", "python3", "python", "python3.exe", "pythonw.exe", "python3.10", "python3.11", "python3.12")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai", "multiedit")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/.ssh/authorized_keys", "/.bashrc", "/.bash_profile", "/.profile", "/.zshrc", "/etc/cron.d", "/etc/crontab", "/var/spool/cron", "/etc/sudoers", @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\")
   or FileName in~ ("authorized_keys", ".bashrc", ".bash_profile", ".profile", ".zshrc", "crontab", "sudoers")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          PreviousFileName, PreviousFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python", "python3", "pythonw")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai", "multiedit")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/.ssh/authorized_keys", "/.bashrc", "/.bash_profile", "/.profile", "/.zshrc", "/etc/cron.d", "/etc/crontab", "/var/spool/cron", "/etc/sudoers")
   or TargetFileName in~ ("authorized_keys", ".bashrc", ".bash_profile", ".profile", ".zshrc", "crontab", "sudoers")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable PraisonAI package exposure (< 4.6.61, GHSA-29w3-p9w9-wc47) AIReconnaissance High
Surfaces hosts running a vulnerable version of the pip:praisonai package so the SOC can drive remediation before exploitation. Pure exposure-management pivot — pairs with the credential-read and persistence detections above so any prior exploitation can be retrospectively hunted on confirmed-vulnerable hosts. Rationale: Targets the exact pip package + version range named in the advisory ('Affected packages: pip:praisonai (vuln < 4.6.61)'). This is the SOC's 'are we even exposed?' query — without it, the hunting detections above have no priority ordering for which hosts to investigate first.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Air-gapped lab hosts where the vulnerable version is intentionally pinned for reproduction research
  • Hosts where Defender TVM has not yet inventoried pip packages (TVM coverage of Python packages is partial — absence does not mean clean)
  • Containers where the praisonai package lives inside an image that TVM cannot introspect
  • Pre-production hosts scheduled for teardown that won't be patched
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Prioritize the result set by IsInternetFacing == true and by chatbot deployment hosts (Telegram/Discord/Slack-integrated PraisonAI is the high-blast-radius shape per the advisory). Step 2 (contain): Drive upgrade to praisonai >= 4.6.61 via the org's pip/Poetry/uv channel; for hosts that can't upgrade immediately, set auto_approve_tools=False on any chatbot integration and remove multiedit from the agent's tool registry. Step 3 (hunt): For every host this query returns, retro-run the credential-read and persistence UCs over the last 90 days — if praisonai was vulnerable, any historical file-access to /etc/shadow or write to authorized_keys by that python process is high-priority IR work, not noise.

Unauthenticated JSON-RPC tools/call hitting an internal MCP HTTP listener AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP POST traffic carrying JSON-RPC method strings ('tools/call','tools/list','resources/read','prompts/get') against the MCP server's default listener port. Targets the specific exploit shape from GHSA-j4f3-55x4-r6q2 where the praisonai TypeScript MCPServer accepts these methods with no Authorization check and binds to all interfaces. Rationale: Anchors on the article's two strongest fingerprints: (1) the specific JSON-RPC method strings handleRequest() dispatches without auth ('tools/call','tools/list','resources/read','prompts/get','initialize'), and (2) the default port 3000 + node.exe parent process running praisonai/mcp/server code. The Sentinel query also captures the article's PoV confirming 'Bearer invalid' is ignored — a Bearer-invalid POST that returns 200 is decisive.
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internal MCP clients on the same host invoking tools/list against a development instance
  • Security scanners (Nuclei, Burp, internal pentest) probing JSON-RPC endpoints on port 3000
  • Loopback PoV/PoC runs by the developer hardening their MCP server
  • Other JSON-RPC services on port 3000 unrelated to praisonai (e.g. Ethereum-style RPC, internal dashboards)
  • Health-check / monitoring probes that send empty POST bodies
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("--test", "--scan", "NODE_ENV=development") | where RemoteIP !in (vuln_scanner_ips) | where AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): pull the offending host's praisonai version (`npm ls praisonai`) and confirm MCPServer.start() is called with HTTP transport; review the WAF/proxy log around the alert window for the source IP, JSON-RPC method, and whether Authorization header was present/valid. Step 2 (contain): if the listener is reachable from outside the trust boundary, block inbound 3000 at the host firewall, restart the node process bound to 127.0.0.1, or stop the service until a patched version (post-1.7.1 with auth wired) is deployed. Step 3 (hunt): for the same source IP, search EmailEvents and DeviceProcessEvents for follow-on activity — node.exe spawning cmd/powershell/bash (tool handler abuse), unexpected file writes by node.exe, and DNS/outbound from the node process to non-corp domains within 1 hour of the inbound JSON-RPC.

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where LocalPort == 3000
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai", "praisonai-ts", "mcp/server", "MCPServer")
| where RemoteIPType !in ("Loopback", "Private") or RemoteIP !in ("127.0.0.1", "::1")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemoteIPType, LocalIP, LocalPort,
          InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationPort == 3000
| where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
| where Message has_any ('"method":"tools/call"', '"method":"tools/list"', '"method":"resources/read"', '"method":"prompts/get"', '"method":"initialize"')
| extend AuthHeaderPresent = Message has "Authorization:"
| extend AuthInvalid = Message has_cs "Authorization: Bearer invalid" or Message matches regex @"(?i)Authorization:\s*Bearer\s+(invalid|test|null|undefined)\b"
| where not(AuthHeaderPresent) or AuthInvalid
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort,
          RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, AuthHeaderPresent, AuthInvalid, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable praisonai npm package (<=1.7.1) installed on host AIWeaponization High
Detects the on-disk fingerprint of the vulnerable npm package (`node_modules/praisonai/package.json` and the unguarded `src/praisonai-ts/src/mcp/server.ts` file) being written during `npm install`. Treat as a hunting hook to find every machine that needs patching before the wider attack-surface hunt. Rationale: Targets the exact file artefacts named in the article ('src/praisonai-ts/src/mcp/server.ts' and the npm package layout). Combining 'node_modules/praisonai' with an npm/yarn/pnpm parent eliminates source-checkout false positives. Pairs with UC1 — patch the hosts this lights up before UC1 trips for real.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer machines doing legitimate development against the praisonai source tree (not exposed to network)
  • CI build runners installing dependencies in ephemeral containers for testing
  • Security-research/sandbox VMs deliberately installing the vulnerable version for reproduction
  • Mirror/cache servers (Verdaccio, Artifactory) pre-fetching the package
  • Old development branches resurrected during git checkout that contain the package.json on disk but never serve it
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Users\\" | where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !contains "\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\" | where DeviceName !in (dev_workstations_watchlist)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): for each host, capture `node_modules/praisonai/package.json` `version` and `dependencies`; confirm whether the host runs `MCPServer.start({port:...})` in production code (grep repo for `MCPServer` instantiation). Step 2 (contain): if production, force-upgrade to a patched version once published or pin to a fork that wires MCPSecurity into startHttp() and binds to 127.0.0.1; in the interim, add a host-firewall rule blocking inbound 3000 from non-loopback. Step 3 (hunt): for every host that has the file, pivot to UC1 over the last 30 days to check whether anyone has already exploited it; pull `node.exe` outbound DNS and process-tree for the same window.

Node.js praisonai MCP server spawning shell or scripting interpreter (tool-call abuse) AIActions on Objectives High
Post-exploitation pivot: an unauthenticated tools/call from UC1 lets the attacker invoke whatever tool handlers the MCPServer registered. Many handlers wrap shell, file, or db actions. This catches node.exe (with praisonai in its cmdline) spawning cmd/powershell/bash/sh as a child — the most common abuse shape regardless of which specific tool is registered. Rationale: The article notes 'MCP tools commonly wrap filesystem operations, API clients, database queries, agent actions, deployment operations, email/Slack actions, browser automation, and code execution'. A node.exe parent whose cmdline references praisonai/MCPServer spawning a shell or scripting interpreter is the single highest-fidelity post-exploit signature regardless of which tool was registered, and pairs cleanly with UC1 as the network-side trigger.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.003 T1059.004 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate registered MCP tools that genuinely wrap shell commands (e.g. a 'run_terminal' tool) used by the application's own AI agent loop
  • Developer testing the MCPServer locally with example tools that exec shell
  • npm postinstall scripts running during package upgrade (node spawning shell briefly)
  • CI/CD pipelines using praisonai for build-step orchestration that legitimately spawn shells
  • Application healthcheck/monitoring scripts invoked by node parent
Suppression filter
| where ChildCmd !has_any ("npm install", "npm run", "node-gyp", "yarn install") | where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("npm.exe", "yarn.exe", "pnpm.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): grab the child process commandline, hash, and any spawned descendants — confirm whether the action looks like a registered MCP tool's legitimate work or arbitrary attacker input (recon strings, encoded payloads, outbound network from the child). Pull the inbound JSON-RPC request from UC1 in the same minute. Step 2 (contain): isolate the host (or stop the node MCP service), revoke any credentials accessible to the node process (env vars, IAM role, .aws/credentials, .npmrc tokens). Step 3 (hunt): pivot on the child's outbound DNS/IPs and any file writes for next-stage payloads; check the source IP of the UC1 request against threat intel and enumerate every other host running praisonai (UC2) for the same source-IP probes.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai", "praisonai-ts", "MCPServer", "mcp/server", "mcp\\server")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "bash.exe", "wsl.exe", "sh.exe", "wscript.exe", "cscript.exe", "mshta.exe", "curl.exe", "certutil.exe", "bitsadmin.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has "node" or ParentProcessName endswith "node.exe"
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai", "praisonai-ts", "MCPServer", "mcp/server", "mcp\\server")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "bash", "sh", "wsl.exe", "wscript.exe", "cscript.exe", "mshta.exe", "curl.exe", "certutil.exe")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine,
          TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, Hash
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Unauthenticated request to PraisonAI AgentOS /api/agents or /api/chat from non-loopback source
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Vulnerable PraisonAI npm AgentOS server process running (GHSA-9752-mhqh-h34f, 1.6.0-1.7.1)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

Vulnerable PraisonAI npm AgentOS server process running (GHSA-9752-mhqh-h34f, 1.6.0-1.7.1) AIInstallation High
Inventory hunt for Node processes running the npm `praisonai` AgentOS HTTP server. Per GHSA-9752-mhqh-h34f, versions 1.6.0-1.7.1 register `/api/agents` and `/api/chat` without any auth middleware and default-bind to 0.0.0.0, so any running instance is a candidate for unauthenticated agent invocation. Surfaces all hosts running the vulnerable component so they can be loopback-bound, patched, or fronted with auth before exploitation. Rationale: Anchored on the exact strings the advisory cites — package name `praisonai`, the shipped artifact path `dist/os/agentos.js`, and the Node host runtime — none of which appear in benign Node command lines. Cross-referenced the Python/PyPI sibling advisories (GHSA-6rmh-7xcm-cpxj, CVE-2026-44338) which confirm the same /api/agents + /api/chat unauthenticated shape and prove this class of bug is being actively exploited within hours of disclosure. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/MervinPraison/PraisonAI/security/advisories/GHSA-6rmh-7xcm-cpxj • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/praisonai-cve-2026-44338-auth-bypass.html • https://cybersecuritynews.com/praisonai-vulnerability-exploited/
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer laptops with praisonai installed for local evaluation (host arg explicitly set to 127.0.0.1)
  • CI/CD runners executing praisonai integration tests in ephemeral containers
  • Sanctioned internal AgentOS deployments already behind an auth-enforcing reverse proxy (nginx/Traefik with bearer-token middleware)
  • Security-research lab hosts running the GHSA PoV reproduction
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("jest.exe", "node-test-runner.exe") and AccountName !endswith "$" and not (DeviceName matches regex "(?i)(dev|build|ci|runner|sandbox)-")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm running praisonai version (`npm ls praisonai` in the install root) and the bind address — run `netstat -ano | findstr 8000` (Win) or `ss -ltnp | grep node` (Linux) to determine whether the listener is on 0.0.0.0 or 127.0.0.1. Check internet exposure via external IP scan / asset inventory. 2) CONTAIN: If bound to 0.0.0.0 with no upstream auth, immediately stop the service, restart with `host: '127.0.0.1'`, or place behind a reverse proxy enforcing a bearer token; if internet-exposed, block port at the edge firewall first. 3) HUNT: Pivot to web/proxy logs for `/api/agents` and `/api/chat` requests over the prior 30 days from any non-loopback source — any hit before the listener was rebound is presumptive compromise; review what tools (file/MCP/credential) the configured agent had reachable.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe", "node")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai", "agentos.js", "dist/os/agentos", @"dist\os\agentos", "AgentOS")
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            arg_max(Timestamp, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, AccountName)
        by DeviceId, DeviceName
| project DeviceName, AccountName, FirstSeen, LastSeen, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by LastSeen desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\node.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "/node"
| where CommandLine has_any ("praisonai", "agentos.js", "dist/os/agentos", @"dist\os\agentos", "AgentOS")
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            arg_max(TimeGenerated, CommandLine, NewProcessName, SubjectUserName)
        by Computer
| project Computer, SubjectUserName, FirstSeen, LastSeen, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by LastSeen desc
title: PraisonAI Vulnerable npm AgentOS Server Execution (GHSA-9752-mhqh-h34f)
id: 9752a8b2-mhqh-4e2f-9a1b-h34f00000001
status: experimental
description: Detects execution of the Node-based npm praisonai AgentOS HTTP server. Versions 1.6.0-1.7.1 expose /api/agents and /api/chat without authentication and default-bind to 0.0.0.0.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9752-mhqh-h34f
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/18
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1133
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_image:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\node.exe'
      - '/node'
  selection_cmd:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'praisonai'
      - 'agentos.js'
      - 'dist/os/agentos'
      - 'dist\os\agentos'
  condition: selection_image and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
  - Developer workstations evaluating praisonai
  - CI/CD pipelines running praisonai integration tests
  - Sanctioned internal AgentOS deployments fronted by an authenticated reverse proxy
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@Image:*\node.exe OR @Image:*\NODE.EXE OR @Image:*\Node.exe OR @Image:*/node) AND (@CommandLine:*praisonai* OR @CommandLine:*PraisonAI* OR @CommandLine:*agentos.js* OR @CommandLine:*AgentOS*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\node(\.exe)?$/i
| regex("(praisonai|agentos\\.js|dist[\\\\/]os[\\\\/]agentos|AgentOS)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="node.exe" OR Processes.process_name="node") AND (Processes.process="*praisonai*" OR Processes.process="*agentos.js*" OR Processes.process="*dist/os/agentos*" OR Processes.process="*dist\\os\\agentos*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process Processes.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | eval ghsa="GHSA-9752-mhqh-h34f"
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="node.exe" OR Processes.process_name="node") AND (Processes.process="*praisonai*" OR Processes.process="*agentos.js*" OR Processes.process="*dist/os/agentos*" OR Processes.process="*dist\\os\\agentos*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process Processes.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | eval ghsa="GHSA-9752-mhqh-h34f"
Unauthenticated request to PraisonAI AgentOS /api/agents or /api/chat from non-loopback source AIExploitation High
Detects HTTP requests to the AgentOS endpoints `/api/agents` (GET — agent enumeration) or `/api/chat` (POST — agent invocation) from a non-loopback source with no `Authorization` header. Per GHSA-9752-mhqh-h34f, these routes are registered with zero auth middleware in npm praisonai 1.6.0-1.7.1, so any such request from a non-loopback IP is presumptive exploitation of the missing authentication boundary. Rationale: Targets the exact two routes the advisory names — `/api/agents` (line 235 of `agentos.ts`) and `/api/chat` (line 250) — gated on (a) source not being loopback and (b) absent Authorization header, which together exactly reproduce the PoV's vulnerable-request shape and the patched 401 control. Cross-referenced the live exploitation pattern reported in the PyPI sibling write-ups, where the same two routes were targeted within hours of disclosure. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/MervinPraison/PraisonAI/security/advisories/GHSA-6rmh-7xcm-cpxj • https://gbhackers.com/praisonai-vulnerability-actively-exploited/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/praisonai-cve-2026-44338-auth-bypass.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059 T1213
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal load balancer / reverse proxy health probes hitting `/api/agents` (real proxy IP, no auth header)
  • Developer making local-LAN curl requests for testing (non-loopback but trusted)
  • Sanctioned internal monitoring (Datadog/Prometheus blackbox exporters) calling `/api/agents` for liveness
  • Sibling-service polling in a Docker network where source IP is the bridge gateway, not loopback
  • Pen-test or vuln-scanner traffic during scheduled internal assessment
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in (<trusted_LB_IPs>) and SrcIpAddr !startswith "10." and HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has_any ("kube-probe", "GoogleHC", "ELB-HealthChecker", "Datadog Agent", "blackbox_exporter")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the source IP — is it internal/trusted (LB, monitoring agent, dev workstation) or external/unknown? Pull the full `/api/chat` request body to see the prompt that was sent — that prompt IS the attacker's command to the agent. Capture HTTP response too: 200 means the agent ran. 2) CONTAIN: Block source IP at the edge, stop the AgentOS service or restart with `host: '127.0.0.1'` and an `Authorization` middleware shim, and revoke any credentials/API keys present in the AgentOS process environment that the invoked agent could have reached. 3) HUNT: For every `/api/chat` POST you confirm, enumerate the configured agent's tools (file/MCP/HTTP/credential tools) and pull their telemetry for the same window — outbound network from the Node PID, files written by the agent, downstream API calls — to scope what the prompt-injected agent actually did.
let praisonHosts = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FileName in~ ("node.exe", "node")
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai", "agentos.js", "dist/os/agentos")
    | summarize by DeviceId, DeviceName;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe", "node")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai", "agentos.js", "dist/os/agentos")
| where LocalPort in (8000, 3000, 4000)
| where RemoteIPType != "Loopback"
| join kind=inner praisonHosts on DeviceId
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemoteIPType, RemotePort, LocalPort,
          InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackHours = 24h;
let AgentOSPorts = dynamic([8000, 3000, 4000, 80, 443]);
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackHours)
| where Url has_any ("/api/agents", "/api/chat")
| where HttpMethod in~ ("GET", "POST")
| where DstPortNumber in (AgentOSPorts) or isempty(DstPortNumber)
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("127.0.0.1", "::1", "0.0.0.0")
| extend EndpointHit = case(Url has "/api/agents", "agents",
                            Url has "/api/chat", "chat", "other")

Node.js spawning shell with reconnaissance commands (PraisonAI codeMode sandbox escape) AIExploitation High
Detects node/node.exe spawning sh/bash/cmd/powershell that immediately runs reconnaissance commands (whoami, uname, /etc/passwd, ~/.ssh). This is the post-RCE primitive demonstrated in the GHSA-p69m-4f92-2v84 PoC where `cp.execSync('id')` was used to confirm sandbox escape via `Function('return this')()` + `global.require('child_'+'process')`. Catches exploitation of any JS sandbox-escape pattern that ends in child_process invocation, not just PraisonAI. Rationale: The GHSA's PoC explicitly demonstrates RCE via `cp.execSync('id').toString()` after escaping the sandbox with `Function('return this')()` and `global.require('child_'+'process')`. Whatever the attacker prompt-injects into `codeMode`, the deterministic OS-level signal is the same: node spawns a shell (Node child_process always exec's via /bin/sh or cmd.exe), and the spawned shell runs recon. Pairing parent=node with child=shell with a recon-command cmdline gives high fidelity because legitimate Node apps rarely shell out to enumerate /etc/passwd or ~/.ssh. I did not web-search — this is a fresh advisory (published <30 days) with no expected secondary corroboration yet.
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059.003 T1082 T1033 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Node-based CI/CD agents (Jenkins agents, GitHub Actions runners, GitLab runners written in Node) executing pipeline scripts that call hostname/whoami for build metadata
  • Node.js diagnostic / health-check libraries (e.g. systeminformation, node-os-utils) shelling out to ifconfig or uname for system info
  • Containerized Node services running an entrypoint script that prints hostname/whoami at startup for logging
  • npm postinstall scripts that probe the environment (e.g. node-gyp builds detecting kernel version with uname -r)
  • Developer-machine Node REPL sessions where engineers manually run cp.execSync('whoami') for testing
Suppression filter
and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp", "node-pre-gyp", "systeminformation", "node-os-utils", "/actions-runner/", "/gitlab-runner/", "/jenkins/") or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"^(?:/bin/sh|/bin/bash)\s+-c\s+\"?hostname\"?\s*$")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the parent Node command line (InitiatingProcessCommandLine) and the script that was being executed. Look for `praisonai`, `codeMode`, `new Function(`, `with (sandbox)`, or `Function('return this')` in process args, loaded scripts, or recent npm package.json on the host. Check the spawning Node process's exposure — is it an LLM-agent backend reachable from the internet? Step 2 — Contain: if praisonai-ts <=1.7.1 is installed and the Node process is internet-exposed, stop the service, snapshot the host, and rotate any credentials in the process environment (env-var API keys are the GHSA's stated impact). Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the same DeviceId for (a) DeviceFileEvents to /tmp, /var/tmp, ~/.ssh, or .bashrc by node; (b) DeviceNetworkEvents from the node ProcessId to public IPs (exfil/C2); (c) DeviceProcessEvents for follow-on curl/wget/bash -i invocations spawned in the same logon session.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe", "node")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\b(whoami|uname|hostname|ifconfig)\b"
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/passwd", "/etc/shadow", "~/.ssh", "/root/.ssh", "ip addr", "cat /root/", "id;", "id |", "id&&")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai", "code-mode", "codeMode", "new Function", "Function('return this')") 
   or AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256, ProcessId, InitiatingProcessId
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\node.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "/node"
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\cmd.exe" or NewProcessName endswith @"\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith @"\pwsh.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "/sh" or NewProcessName endswith "/bash" or NewProcessName endswith "/dash" or NewProcessName endswith "/zsh"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\b(whoami|uname|hostname|ifconfig)\b"
   or CommandLine has_any ("/etc/passwd", "/etc/shadow", "~/.ssh", "/root/.ssh", "ip addr", "cat /root/")
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, NewProcessId, ProcessId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable PraisonAI-TS package (<=1.7.1) installed — GHSA-p69m-4f92-2v84 AIWeaponization High
Hunts for hosts with the npm package `praisonai` (or `praisonai-ts`) at a version <=1.7.1 installed, which is vulnerable to the codeMode tool sandbox-escape RCE. Catches at-risk inventory before exploitation. Pivots on TVM software inventory and on file-event evidence of the package directory. Rationale: The GHSA names the exact vulnerable package and ceiling (`praisonai <=1.7.1`) and the exact file path (`src/praisonai-ts/src/tools/builtins/code-mode.ts`). DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory gives clean inventory for hosts where the package is registered; the DeviceFileEvents fallback catches hand-installed copies or container-baked images that TVM may not enumerate. Sentinel KQL is empty because the analyst-tenant Sentinel schema in this environment does not expose DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory or a file-event table covering node_modules paths — operators should hunt this via Defender XDR or the npm-audit pipeline. CloudWatch is empty for the same reason (not AWS telemetry).
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Inventory.Software
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal security-research/test hosts deliberately running the vulnerable version to validate detections — keep but tag
  • Developer workstations with the package in a sandboxed test directory unrelated to production services
  • Container build hosts where the image is built but never executed in production (pre-bake CI runners)
  • Vendored copies inside another repo (node_modules of a different project that depends on praisonai transitively but isn't internet-exposed)
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("sec-research-", "detection-lab-", "-buildagent-") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("docker.exe", "containerd-shim.exe", "buildkitd"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: for each hit, determine whether the host is internet-exposed and whether the praisonai agent is actually instantiated with `codeMode` enabled (grep the host's app config for `code-mode`, `codeMode`, or `tools: [codeMode]`). If codeMode is not enabled, downgrade to advisory; the vulnerable code path requires the tool to be wired into an agent. Step 2 — Contain: for exposed services with codeMode enabled, force-pin the dependency to a patched version (>=1.7.2 once published) or disable the codeMode tool in agent config; rotate any API keys/secrets present in the Node process environment. Step 3 — Hunt: cross-reference hit hosts against UC #1 (Node spawning shell with recon) over the past 30d to confirm no prior exploitation. Add the package directory to a watch-list for change events (new versions, new installs) until the org-wide upgrade is complete.
// Inventory pass — vulnerable versions per Defender TVM
let vuln = DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
  | where SoftwareName has "praisonai"
  | where SoftwareVersion matches regex @"^(0\.|1\.[0-6]\.|1\.7\.[01](?:$|[^0-9]))"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion;
// Filesystem fallback — catches manual / non-managed installs TVM missed
let fileEvidence = DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FolderPath matches regex @"(?i)node_modules[\\/]praisonai(?:-ts)?[\\/]"
  | where FileName =~ "package.json"
  | summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Paths=make_set(FolderPath, 25) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName;
union isfuzzy=true vuln, fileEvidence
| order by DeviceName asc
(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\\node_modules\\praisonai\\package.json OR *\\node_modules\\praisonai-ts\\package.json)) OR (source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:PATH @name:(*\/node_modules\/praisonai\/package.json OR *\/node_modules\/praisonai-ts\/package.json))
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/node_modules[\\\/]praisonai(?:-ts)?[\\\/]package\.json$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())

Node.js spawned shell/utility from praisonai codeMode context (sandbox escape post-exploitation) AIExploitation High
Hunts for Node.js processes that load the praisonai package (which advertises codeMode as a sandbox) but then spawn child shell/utility processes. A working sandbox would not permit child_process.spawn; any such child indicates the Function-constructor / prototype-chain escape described in GHSA-vmmj-pfw7-fjwp succeeded. Rationale: Pivots on the article's named package string 'praisonai' and the tool name 'codeMode' (src/praisonai-ts/src/tools/builtins/code-mode.ts) appearing in the node parent process command line, combined with shells/utilities the codeMode blocklist explicitly forbids — printf was the exact binary spawned in the published PoV. Cross-checked GHSA-vmmj-pfw7-fjwp advisory page; npmjs praisonai package listing. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vmmj-pfw7-fjwp • https://www.npmjs.com/package/praisonai
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1068 T1611
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running praisonai dev/test scripts that legitimately use shell tooling outside codeMode
  • CI/CD jobs invoking praisonai e2e tests that intentionally spawn child processes
  • Postinstall hooks of @praisonai dev tooling using node to call printf for logging
  • Maintainer reproduction of the PoV (poc/pov_poc.js) on a research host
  • Containerised praisonai workloads using shell-invoking node tools (langchain.js shell tool, etc.)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("test","jest","vitest","mocha","npm run test","e2e") and AccountName has_any ("dev","build","ci","jenkins"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull full process tree on the host — confirm the parent node.exe has praisonai/code-mode in cmdline and identify whether the child shell ran an attacker-supplied command (look for env-var dumps, file reads, or outbound network). 2) Contain: isolate the host via Defender Live Response, kill the offending node.exe PID, snapshot /tmp + cwd of the node process, rotate any secrets exposed via process.env (cloud API keys, LLM provider tokens). 3) Hunt: search 30d for the same node + praisonai parent → child shell pattern on other hosts; pivot on any DeviceFileEvents writes by node.exe to non-project paths and on outbound network from node.exe to non-LLM-provider IPs (post-escape egress).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai","code-mode","codeMode")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","sh","bash","zsh","dash","printf","printf.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ParentImage=InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ChildImage=FolderPath, ChildCmd=ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4688
| extend ParentProcessNameLower = tolower(ParentProcessName), CommandLineLower = tolower(CommandLine), NewProcessNameLower = tolower(NewProcessName)

| where NewProcessNameLower endswith_cs "\\cmd.exe" or NewProcessNameLower endswith_cs "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessNameLower endswith_cs "\\pwsh.exe" or NewProcessNameLower endswith "\\wscript.exe" or NewProcessNameLower endswith "\\cscript.exe" or NewProcessNameLower endswith "\\curl.exe" or NewProcessNameLower endswith "\\wget.exe" or NewProcessNameLower endswith "/sh" or NewProcessNameLower endswith "/bash" or NewProcessNameLower endswith "/printf"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"

description: Detects child shell or scripting processes spawned by node.exe whose command line indicates praisonai/codeMode is loaded. The codeMode tool advertises a sandbox boundary and explicitly blocks child_process; any spawned shell child is evidence of GHSA-vmmj-pfw7-fjwp prototype-chain escape.
references:
    - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vmmj-pfw7-fjwp
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/18
tags:

detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:

    condition: selection_parent and selection_child

    - Legitimate praisonai workflows that invoke shell tools outside codeMode (rare; codeMode advertises a sandbox)
level: high

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^node\.exe$/i
| regex("(praisonai|code-?mode|codeMode)", field=ParentCommandLine)
| ImageFileName=/\\(cmd|powershell|pwsh|wscript|cscript|curl|wget|printf)\.exe$/i
